exp.1:29:
He says that Epaphroditus came close to dying because of his work for Christ. He risked his life to complete the help that the Philippians had not been able to give Paul in person. The phrase "to supply your lack of service" means making up for what you could not do, that is, being with Paul and serving him.

Paul writes from prison. The Philippians had sent Epaphroditus with a gift and to assist him. Epaphroditus fell seriously ill and is now returning home. Paul wants him to be received with joy and honor, and does not want them to think he came back out of weakness or failure. The letter does not give all the details of his illness.

Today we can value and encourage those who serve with sacrifice and without seeking applause: pastors, volunteers, teachers, or caregivers. A word of gratitude, a prayer, or a concrete help can strengthen them. And we too can serve with simple devotion.
exp.1:10:
It says that everyone, without exception, will openly acknowledge that Jesus Christ is Lord. "Every tongue" means every person, and "confess" means to declare openly. This declaration does not end with Jesus alone, but brings glory to God the Father.

Paul writes to the Philippians from prison. Before this, he speaks of Christ, who humbled himself even to death on the cross, and God exalted him. He wants to encourage them to live with humility and unity. Some believe this passage was an ancient Christian hymn, although this cannot be known for certain. Interpreters debate whether everyone will confess out of faith or out of forced recognition.

For today: if Jesus is Lord, you can hand him your daily decisions. Today, in one specific matter, stop insisting on getting your own way and serve him with humility, as he did.
exp.3:15:
Paul recalls that the Philippians helped him even while he was in Thessalonica. They sent what was needed to live, and not just once, but more than one time, on more than one occasion.

Paul writes this letter from prison, and thanks the Philippians for their generous help. He reminds them that, when he began his work in Macedonia, they were the only ones who shared with him in this way. He is not asking for more money; he wants them to see that their generosity pleases God and bears fruit.

For today: do not underestimate steady, simple help. Supporting a missionary, a pastor, or someone in need, again and again, is a service that God sees and values.
exp.1:2:
This verse asks us not to act out of quarrelsome rivalry or selfish ambition, nor out of a desire to show off or to win applause. Instead, we should act with humility, regarding others as more important than ourselves.

Paul writes from prison to the church in Philippi, which he loves dearly. He asks them for unity, and says his joy will be complete when he sees them loving one another and thinking in harmony. This verse prepares the example of Christ, who humbled himself for the sake of others (vv. 5-8).

Today, before you give your opinion, argue a point, or post something, ask yourself: "Am I doing this to serve, or to make myself look good?" This week, look for a concrete opportunity to listen carefully to someone, or to give another person the credit, without seeking recognition for yourself.
exp.2:9:
What it says: Paul expresses his great desire to know Christ in a deep and personal way. He wants to experience "the power of his resurrection," that is, the power by which God raised Jesus. He also wants "the fellowship of his sufferings," sharing in his sufferings, and to be "made conformable unto his death," that is, to become like Christ in his self-giving and humility.

Context: Paul writes from prison to the Philippians. He has just said that all his former achievements are worth nothing compared with Christ. His goal is not to boast of perfection, for he immediately clarifies that he is still pressing forward. Some understand "conformable unto his death" as dying to the self; others, as being willing to be martyred.

For today: Instead of seeking only a comfortable faith, ask God to know Christ more closely. When a difficulty comes from following him, remember that the same power that raised him can sustain you.
exp.2:3:
Paul says that he too would have reason to put confidence in the flesh, that is, in his human achievements, his background, and his religious effort. And he adds that if anyone thinks he has more reason to boast in these things, he has even more. To have confidence in the flesh means to rely on what a person is or does, instead of relying on God.

Paul writes to the Philippians from prison. He warns them against teachers who insisted that believers had to keep Jewish rites, such as circumcision, in order to be accepted by God. To answer them, Paul shows that his religious record was impeccable. Then he explains that he considers it loss compared with knowing Christ.

Today we can ask ourselves where we rest in order to feel valued before God: in our church, our good works, or our reputation? God accepts us through the grace of Christ, and that allows us to live with humility and gratitude.
exp.2:19:
It says that our "home," that is, our citizenship or the place we truly belong to, is in heaven. The Greek word behind it has to do with being a citizen of a place. From there, we eagerly wait for the Savior to come, the Lord Jesus Christ.

Paul writes to the Philippians from prison. He has just spoken sadly about people who live only for earthly things, and this verse sets that contrast in place. Philippi was a Roman colony, so his readers understood well what it meant to have citizenship in another place. The verses that follow say that Christ will transform our body.

For today: if your true homeland is in heaven, you can live with less anxiety about what passes away. Today, when you decide how to use your time or your money, ask yourself: "Does this show that I belong to Christ?"
exp.3:13:
Paul tells the Philippians that they did well to share in his suffering. The phrase "that ye did communicate with my affliction" means that they took part with him, sharing in his need. Although he had learned to be content in any situation, he warmly acknowledges what they did.

Paul writes this letter from prison, probably in Rome, though some think it was another place. The Philippians had sent him help through Epaphroditus. Paul thanks them without suggesting that he depends on them, since he has just said that his strength comes from Christ. In this way he values their generosity and their love.

Today we can support someone going through a hard time, with a visit, a phone call, a prayer, or material help. And if someone helps us, let us thank them sincerely.
exp.3:12:
Paul says that he can face whatever life brings because Christ gives him strength. "I can do all things" does not mean that he can achieve anything he wants, but that he can meet any situation. "Which strengtheneth me" means that Christ continually gives him encouragement and power.

Paul writes this letter to the Philippians from prison. He thanks them for the financial help they sent him. He makes clear that he is not speaking out of need, for he has learned to be content both with plenty and with little. His strength does not come from his circumstances, but from Christ.

Today, when you face scarcity, abundance, or a hard trial, do not depend only on your own strength. Ask Christ to give you patience, gratitude, and steadfastness so that you can live each season with faith and peace.
exp.0:15:
These words describe some who preached Christ out of contention, that is, out of rivalry and a desire to argue. They were not doing it sincerely, but with bad intent. They thought that by doing so they would make Paul's situation in prison harder to bear. The words "bonds" and "add affliction" in the verse mean chains or imprisonment, and causing him more suffering.

Paul writes from prison to the Philippians. He tells them that his imprisonment has encouraged many brothers to speak the word boldly. But others preached out of envy. Even so, Paul rejoices that Christ is being proclaimed. We do not know in detail who these preachers were or exactly what they were seeking.

For today: let us examine our motives in serving God. Let it not be for competition or self-display, but out of love. And when we see others proclaiming Christ, even if they are not like us, let us learn to rejoice that the gospel is advancing.
exp.2:8:
Paul says he wants to be "found in Christ," that is, united with him. He does not want to rely on his own righteousness, meaning being right with God through keeping the law of Moses. He wants the righteousness that comes from believing in Christ, the kind God himself gives. To be "found" means to be discovered or recognized, and "through the faith of Christ" can be understood as trust in Christ.

Paul writes to the believers in Philippi, probably from prison. Earlier he mentions his religious achievements, which he could have been proud of. Now he says that all of that is worth nothing compared with knowing Christ. He may also want to warn the Philippians against those who put their trust in the works of the law.

Today, we can stop presenting our merits to God, such as being good, going to church, or helping others. Those things have value, but they do not save us. We can rest in the fact that Christ presents us as righteous before God, and obey with gratitude, not with fear.
exp.1:18:
Paul says that he hopes, if the Lord Jesus allows it, to send Timothy to the Philippians soon. In this way Paul would also be encouraged when he learns how they are doing. The word "shortly" means soon, and "when I know your state" means "when I learn how you are doing."

Paul writes from prison, and he does not know whether he will be set free or will die. Even so, he thinks about the good of the church in Philippi. His statement "I trust in the Lord Jesus" shows that he depends on God for his plans. Then he praises Timothy as someone who truly cares for them.

For today: Look after others with sincere interest. Ask how they are, listen, and help, and place your plans in God's hands. Even in difficult times, practical love for others encourages the heart.
exp.3:4:
This verse asks that everyone see in us a kind, gentle, and patient attitude. The word "gentleness" here does not refer to clothing, but to being calm, reasonable, and gracious in how we treat others, without always insisting on our own rights. It adds a reason: "The Lord is at hand." This can be understood as meaning that Christ will come soon, or that God is present with us now; both ideas fit.

Paul writes to the Philippians from prison. He speaks to them about joy in the Lord and about disagreements among brothers and sisters. Shortly before, he has asked for help for two women who worked alongside him in the gospel. Afterward he encourages them not to live in anxiety, but to pray.

For today: when you become angry or feel pressured, before you respond, take a breath and remember that the Lord is near, and answer with calm and kindness, even if others do not agree with you.
exp.1:11:
Paul calls the Philippians "my beloved" and commends them because they have always obeyed, not only when he was with them, but even more now that he is far away. He asks them to work out their salvation, that is, to live it out and grow in it, with fear and trembling, which means seriousness, humility, and reverence toward God.

Paul writes from prison. He has just spoken of Christ, who humbled himself and was exalted by God. Now he encourages them to live out that same humility. He does not say they must earn salvation: the next verse makes clear that it is God who works in them both the willing and the doing.

Today we can take our faith seriously even when no one sees us. Set aside a moment each day to pray and to obey God in something concrete, trusting that He gives you the strength to do it.
exp.1:27:
Paul says that he is sending Epaphroditus back to Philippi with greater haste. His purpose is that the Philippians may rejoice when they see him again, and that Paul may be the less sorrowful, that is, less anxious and grieved.

Paul writes from prison. Epaphroditus had brought Paul the help sent by the Philippians, and there he became so ill that he nearly died. The Philippians heard of this and grieved for him, and he grieved for them. In sending him, Paul seeks the good of everyone and asks that they receive him with joy.

For today: when someone worries about others, we can lighten their burden with a visit, a phone call, or a message. Our joy in being reunited and caring for one another is a real expression of Christian love.
exp.1:3:
It says that we should not think only of our own interests, but also of the interests of others. The word "look" means to fix one's attention, and "on his own things" refers to what is personally convenient for us. It is not wrong to take care of what is our own; what is corrected is living only for that.

The apostle Paul writes from prison to the believers in Philippi, whom he loves dearly. He asks them for unity, humility, and that they avoid quarrels and the desire to stand out. This verse prepares the example that follows: Christ, who being equal with God, did not cling to his position, but served others.

For today: before making a decision at home, at work, or in the church, ask yourself: "How does this affect the other person?" Then do something concrete, such as listening carefully or helping someone without expecting anything in return.
exp.0:17:
Paul asks: "What then?" It does not matter whether Christ is proclaimed with wrong motives or with sincerity; what matters is that he is proclaimed. That is why he rejoices, and he will go on rejoicing. The verse's "rejoice" and "will rejoice" carry this same sense of gladness.

Paul writes from prison, probably in Rome, though some scholars think of another place. Some preachers did it out of rivalry, hoping to make his imprisonment harder; others did it out of love. Paul is not concerned with his own comfort or reputation, but with the message of Christ reaching more people.

Today we can rejoice when Christ is proclaimed, even when it is not done our way or by people we like. May envy and pride not win out in us. Let us ask God for a heart that puts Jesus first.
exp.0:11:
Paul tells the Philippians that he wants them to know something important. The word "fallen out" means that something turned out to result in something else; here, that his troubles served to make the gospel advance further. "Furtherance" means benefit or progress.

Paul writes this letter from prison, probably in Rome, though some scholars have thought of other places. The Philippians loved him dearly and worried about him. Paul reassures them: his imprisonment, which seemed like a setback, was opening doors to proclaim Christ, as the following verses show.

When you go through a difficulty, do not think only about how much it hurts. Ask God how He can use it for the good of others. Perhaps your way of responding, with peace and faith, will speak of Christ to those who watch you.
exp.0:8:
Paul prays that the love of the Philippians will grow more and more, and that this love will be joined with knowledge and with judgment. In this case, knowledge does not refer to laboratories or school learning, but to a correct understanding of what God is and what he wants. Abound means to overflow, to grow greatly.

Paul writes from prison to a church that has supported him with affection and faithfulness. He has just told them how much he loves them. Now he prays for them, and his desire is that their love be wise, so that they can discern what is best and live with sincerity until the day of Christ.

For today: love is not just a pleasant feeling. Ask God to make your love grow, and feed that love by reading the Bible and learning to decide wisely how to truly help others.
exp.0:23:
What it says: Paul states that continuing to live in this body is more necessary for the Philippians. "Nevertheless" means "but," and "to remain in the flesh" means to stay alive on earth. "For your sake" means "for you."

Context: Paul writes this letter from prison. He is torn between two desires: to die and be with Christ, which he considers "far better," or to stay alive to help the churches. Here he decides to think about the needs of the believers in Philippi. He then expresses his confidence that he will see them again and encourage them in their faith.

For today: God keeps us here with a purpose. Each day we can ask ourselves whom I can serve, encourage, or accompany. Living is not only waiting for heaven; it is also loving others with the time God gives us.
exp.0:9:
Paul asks that the Philippians be able to tell the best apart, that is, to choose what is most worthwhile and pleasing to God, and not merely what seems good. He also wants them to be "sincere," meaning pure-hearted and honest, and "without offence," which means without stumbling or blame, and not causing others to fall. All of this is to be held in view of "the day of Christ," when Jesus returns and judges.

Paul writes from prison to a church he loves dearly. In the verses just before, he prays that their love will grow in knowledge and good judgment. This verse shows the purpose: that love be mature and not blind.

For today: before deciding something, don't ask only whether it is wrong or permitted, but what is best. Ask God for wisdom, check whether your motives are honest, and consider whether your decision helps or hinders others.
exp.1:22:
Paul says he hopes to send Timothy to the Philippians as soon as he sees how things will turn out with his circumstances, that is, how his situation is resolved. The phrase "as soon as I shall see" means that Paul will send Timothy right after he knows the outcome of his own case; and "how it will go with me" refers to his affairs, especially his trial while he was in prison.

Paul writes from prison, and most people think he was in Rome, though some suggest another place. He has just praised Timothy, who, unlike others, was not looking out for his own interests but served Paul like a son serving his father. That is why he wants to send him, but first he needs to know how his case will go.

For today: serve with a willing heart, but also with patience. Paul makes plans, but he waits to see how things become clear. We can trust God while we wait for his direction.
exp.3:11:
Paul says he knows how to live with little and also with plenty. Here "abased" means going through lack or need, not feeling lesser. "Full" means being well fed, having everything necessary. He has learned to stay at peace both when he has more than enough and when he lacks food or resources.

The apostle Paul writes from prison to the Philippians, who sent him help through Epaphroditus. He thanks them for their affection, but makes clear that his joy does not depend on the gift. His contentment is something he learned over time, and it is sustained by the strength of Christ, as he says in the following verse.

Today, both in times of plenty and in times of scarcity, we can ask God for a grateful heart. When something is lacking, avoid comparing yourself to others; when you have more than enough, share generously and do not place your security in what you have.
exp.1:17:
Paul invites the Philippians to rejoice, and asks them to be glad together with him. Joy is something that is shared.

Paul writes this letter from prison. In the verse before, he says that even if his life is poured out as a drink offering (like a cup of wine poured out in a sacrifice), he is glad. It is a picture of giving oneself completely, perhaps even to death. He does not want them to mourn for him, but to share his joy in having served God.

For today: even in difficult times, we can choose to give thanks and rejoice in God. Share that joy with other believers; encourage one another and remember that serving the Lord is never in vain.
exp.3:20:
Paul asks that every saint in Christ Jesus be greeted, that is, every believer in the church, leaving no one out. "Saints" does not refer to perfect people but to those set apart for God. The phrase "salute every saint" is what the verse says. Then he says that the brethren who are with him also send their greetings.

Paul writes this letter to the Philippians from prison, probably in Rome, as the final note of this edition indicates, although some scholars have proposed other places. He closes the letter with a warm gesture. After speaking of God's provision and giving him glory, he shows that faith is also lived out in friendship and in the unity between churches.

Today we can imitate this gesture: send a message, make a phone call, or give a sincere greeting to brothers and sisters in the faith, especially to those who feel lonely or forgotten. A simple greeting reminds us that we belong to one family in Christ.
exp.0:19:
Paul says he firmly expects that he will not be ashamed in anything. On the contrary, he trusts that Christ will be magnified, that is, shown to be great, in his body, whether Paul remains alive or dies.

Paul writes to the Philippians from prison. Some were preaching Christ with doubtful motives, but he rejoices that the message is advancing. He does not know whether he will be released or put to death, and yet his aim is that Christ be honored in either case.

Today we can ask not only "How will I get out of this situation?" but "How can Christ be honored in it?" At work, in illness, or in trial, we can pray this way: "Lord, may my manner of living and of facing this show you to be great."
exp.2:4:
Paul lists his religious credentials. He was circumcised on the eighth day after his birth, as the law commanded. He belonged to the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, and he was a Hebrew of Hebrews, meaning a son of Hebrew parents who kept their language and customs. As for the law, he was a Pharisee, a member of the group most strict in keeping it.

Paul writes from prison to the Christians in Philippi. He warns them against those who trusted in rituals and heritage to please God. To show that he is not speaking out of envy, he reminds them that he had more reasons than anyone to boast. Soon he will say that he counted all of that as loss compared with Christ.

For today: family, church, or good works are not enough to be right with God. Be thankful for what you have, but rest only in Christ.
exp.1:16:
Paul says that, even if his life is poured out like a drink offering (libation) on the sacrifice the Philippians offer to God through their faith, he rejoices and congratulates them all.

Paul writes from prison, not knowing whether he will come out alive. He calls the Philippians' life of faith a sacrifice and service. His possible death would be like the wine poured out at the end of an offering: something that accompanies and completes what they are already giving. Paul encourages them to shine like lights in the middle of a dark world.

Today we can serve God and others with joy, even when it costs time, comfort, or effort. If we rejoice in the good of others and not only in our own, service becomes lighter and full of gladness.
exp.0:5:
Paul says he is sure of something: that God, who began a good work in the Philippians, will carry it through to its goal. The phrase "will perform it" means he will complete it and bring it to its full result. The "day of Jesus Christ" refers to the moment when Christ returns, when everything will be fulfilled.

Paul writes from prison to the church in Philippi, which had supported him in the gospel from the very beginning. He thanks them and prays for them with joy. His confidence does not rest on their strength but on God, who was the one who started that work. Some think the "good work" includes their faith and their generosity; the text does not spell this out.

For today: if you feel tired or think you have made little progress in your life with God, rest in the fact that He does not abandon what He begins. Keep obeying, and trust that He is still at work in you.
exp.0:13:
Many believers, seeing Paul in prison, were encouraged instead of frightened. For that reason they spoke God's message with much more boldness and without fear. The chains or the imprisonment are what the verse refers to by "bonds." To have the courage to do it is what waxing confident means. The message is the gospel, the message of Jesus.

Paul writes this letter to the Philippians from prison, probably in Rome, although some think it may have been another place. He wants to reassure them: his imprisonment did not stop the gospel, but advanced it. His example of steadfast faith encouraged other brothers and sisters, who lost their fear.

For today: our faith in the middle of difficulties can give courage to others. When you face a trial, trust God and keep bearing witness simply. Your attitude may encourage someone else to speak about Christ without fear.
exp.3:3:
This verse invites us to rejoice in the Lord at all times. Paul repeats it for emphasis: "and again I say." "Rejoice" means to be glad, and the repeated command is a gentle call to live with joy. Joy is not placed in circumstances, but in the Lord himself.

Paul writes to the Philippians from prison, and yet he speaks of joy. Shortly before, he asked Euodia and Syntyche to live in harmony, since there was tension in the church. Then he speaks of being gentle, of not being anxious, and of prayer. Joy appears here as a steady attitude, not as a passing feeling.

Today, when something weighs on you, before you complain, stop and remember who the Lord is and what he has done for you. Thank him for one specific thing. In this way your heart begins to rest in him, even if the problem remains.
exp.3:2:
It says that Paul asks a "true yokefellow" to help the women who labored with him in the gospel. It also mentions Clement and his other fellow workers. "I intreat" means I ask, and "help" means support those women. At the end it states that their names are "in the book of life," meaning God counts them as his own.

Paul writes from prison to the church at Philippi. Just before this, he asked Euodias and Syntyche to agree with each other. Now he asks someone to help them be reconciled. We do not know who this "yokefellow" is; some think he is a specific person, and others think he is any co-worker in the church. Nothing more is known about this Clement either.

For today: when two brothers and sisters in the faith are in conflict, do not judge them or leave them alone. Help with humility, listening and praying, and remember how much they have served God.
exp.1:13:
Paul asks us to do everything without complaints and without arguments. "Complaints" are the quiet grumbling, the constant griping. "Arguments" are the quarrels and fights to be proven right. He means everything we do, not just the easy things.

Paul writes to the believers in Philippi from prison. He has just spoken to them about obeying and about God himself working in them. Then he explains the purpose: that they be blameless and shine like lights in the middle of a crooked world. Some see here a reminder of Israel's complaints in the desert, though the text does not state this clearly.

Today: the next time you feel like complaining at work, at home, or at church, stop and pray. Ask God for help to do your task with a good attitude, so that the way you live will show others a bit of his light.
exp.1:6:
The explanation says that Jesus "made himself of no reputation", that is, he set aside or emptied himself, not of his divinity, but of his position of glory and his rights. He took "the form of a servant" and became like men. The word "made himself of no reputation" is an old one; other translations say "emptied himself" or "stripped himself". Christians explain in various ways what this emptying exactly means, but all agree that it was a voluntary act of humility.

Paul writes from prison to the Philippians, a church he loved very much. He asks them for unity and humility, and to make the point he sets Christ before them as an example. The previous verse says that Jesus was equal with God and did not cling to that; here we see what he did instead.

Today, this invites us to serve without seeking recognition. Think of a situation where you could demand your place or insist that you are right, and decide instead to serve that person with patience and kindness.
exp.0:6:
Paul says it is right for him to think this way about all the Philippians, because he holds them in his heart. Whether he is in chains, defending the gospel, or confirming it, they have been "partakers of my grace" with him, that is, sharers with him in the favor God gave him.

Paul writes to the church in Philippi from prison, probably in Rome, though some think it was another place. He has just thanked them and expressed confidence that God will finish the work he has begun in them. Here he explains why he cares for them so much: they supported him and shared in his mission, even in hard times.

For today: walk alongside others in their service and in their trials. Pray for, help, visit, or encourage someone who is going through a difficulty because of their faith. In this way we too share in the grace of God.
exp.0:24:
Paul says that he is convinced he will remain alive and will stay with the Philippians. He does this for their benefit and so that their faith may grow with joy. The words "remain" and "stay" mean that he will not die for now. "Progress" means advantage, and "joy of faith" is the gladness that comes from trusting God.

Paul writes from prison and does not know whether he will be released or put to death. He has just said that he desires to be with Christ, but he feels it is more necessary for him to keep living for their sake. His confidence grows out of that love for the church. Some scholars point out that this is a personal conviction and not a certain prophecy.

For today: ask yourself how you can use your days, your health, and your time to help others grow in faith. Living with that purpose gives meaning even to the difficult seasons.
exp.1:1:
Paul asks the Philippians to "fulfil" his joy, that is, to make it complete. This happens when they think alike, have the same love, and are "of one accord," meaning united in heart. "Being of one mind" means having the same purpose and the same attitude.

Paul writes this letter from prison, and yet he speaks of joy. Earlier he reminded them of what they already have in Christ: comfort, love, fellowship in the Spirit, and tenderness. For that reason he asks them for unity. The verses that follow show that the problem was selfishness and rivalry. Unity does not mean thinking identically about everything, but going together toward the same goal: living for Christ.

Today, in the family, at work, or in the church, let us seek peace before we seek to be right. Before answering in an argument, ask yourself: what helps us stay united in Christ and serving together?
exp.0:21:
Paul says that if continuing to live in this body means more fruit from his work for the Lord, then he does not know what to choose. "To live in the flesh" means to remain alive here on earth. The "fruit of labour" is the good result of his service. "To choose" means to pick between living or dying.

Paul writes this letter from prison, not knowing whether he will be set free or die. He is speaking to the Philippians, whom he loves. For him, dying is gain because he would be with Christ, but living allows him to keep serving and helping them. The verses that follow show that he feels torn between these two desires.

Today we can learn to see life as an opportunity to serve, not only to fulfill our own wishes. We can ask God to help us live with purpose and, at the same time, to trust that being with Him is best.
exp.2:15:
It says that, as far as we have already advanced in faith, we should keep walking along the same path and with the same mindset. "Nevertheless" means "but," and "rule" is the standard or pattern we follow. It is not about standing still, but about moving forward without abandoning what we have already learned.

Paul writes to the Christians in Philippi from prison. He has just said that he keeps pressing toward the goal, without thinking he has arrived. Now he invites the mature believers to have that same attitude. Right after, he asks them to follow his example and warns them against those who live as enemies of the cross.

For today: you do not need to start from zero each day. Hold on to what you already know of Christ, obey him with steadiness, and seek unity with your brothers and sisters, even while you are still growing.
exp.1:8:
God the Father lifted Jesus up to the highest place. The phrase "exalted to the utmost" means that he raised him to the highest degree. He also gave him a name above every other name. According to verse 11, this name is "Lord." Some understand that it also refers to the name of Jesus, and scholars have interpreted this in several ways.

Paul writes to the believers in Philippi from prison. He asks them for humility and unity. Earlier he presented Christ to them, who humbled himself even to death on a cross. The words "Wherefore" connect both things: because of that obedient humility, God exalted him.

For today: we do not have to fight to be seen or to be right. Jesus showed that serving with humility is not losing, and God knows how to honor in his time. Today you can choose to serve someone quietly, trusting that God sees.
exp.2:16:
Paul asks the believers to follow his example. He also tells them to watch closely those who live according to the pattern they received from Paul and his companions.

Paul writes to the church in Philippi, probably from prison. He has just said that he is still moving forward toward Christ and does not consider himself perfect. Now he invites them to grow together with that same attitude. Afterward he warns them against those who live as enemies of the cross, thinking only about earthly things.

Today we can look for humble people who live with faith and love, and learn from their example. We are also called to live in such a way that others see Christ in us. Ask yourself: whom am I following, and what example am I setting?
exp.0:12:
Paul says that his imprisonment became very well known, and that everyone came to know he was in prison for the sake of Christ. The words "bonds" (the chains of his imprisonment) and "well known" (meaning widely recognized and talked about) are explained as follows: "bonds" means chains or imprisonment, and "well known" means widely recognized or notorious. The "palace" probably refers to the imperial guard or the governor's headquarters; scholars do not fully agree on which it was. The phrase "and all the others" refers to other people who found out.

Paul writes to the Philippians from prison, probably in Rome, though some think of another place. His friends could fear that his imprisonment had slowed the gospel. He reassures them: what happened has instead helped it advance, since even the guards came to know why he was imprisoned.

For today: when you face a difficulty you did not choose, ask God whom you can serve or where you can bear witness right there. He can use even your trials to show Christ.
exp.0:3:
Paul says that every time he prays, he always prays for all the Philippians, and he does it with joy. "Always in every prayer of mine" means that he does not stop remembering them when he prays. The explanation of "you all" as an old form of "you" and the note on "making request" are left out, since those words do not appear in the verse your reader sees.

Paul writes this letter from prison, according to what he himself tells us in the letter. Even so, his tone is one of thankfulness, not complaint. The Philippians had supported him and shared with him the work of proclaiming the gospel, and so remembering them gave him joy. The next verse explains the reason: their partnership in the gospel, that is, their fellowship in God's work.

Today we can do something similar: think of the people who have been a blessing in our lives and pray for them with thanksgiving. Praying for others with gratitude, and not only with worry, changes our hearts and fills us with joy.
exp.3:7:
It says that, finally, believers should fix their minds on what is good. "Honest" here means worthy and respectable; "lovely" means worthy of being loved; "of good report" refers to what has a good reputation; "virtue" means moral excellence. "Think on" means to meditate on, to take into account with careful attention.

Paul writes this letter to the Philippians, probably while in prison. Just before this, he asked them not to live anxiously but to pray with thanksgiving. Now he shows them the next step: besides praying, they must be careful about what occupies their thoughts. Then he invites them to imitate what they saw in him.

For today: when worry or the news fills you with anguish, pause, pray, and deliberately choose something good to think about. For example, write down three true and good things from your day and thank God for them.
exp.3:0:
Paul calls the Philippians "brethren, dearly beloved and longed for", that is, people he loves deeply and misses. He says they are his "joy and crown": his happiness and his reason for pride, like the prize of an athlete. He asks them to "stand fast in the Lord", meaning that they should not waver in their faith. The word "therefore" points back to what he has just taught: that their true citizenship is in heaven.

Paul writes this letter from prison to the church in Philippi, which he himself helped to found. He speaks to them with the affection of a pastor. Soon he will ask two women, Euodia and Syntyche, to live in harmony, so the steadfastness he asks for includes unity.

For today: standing firm in faith is not lived alone. Think of someone in your church or family with whom there is distance, and take one concrete step toward peace, such as a phone call or a prayer for that person.
exp.0:29:
Paul says that the Philippians are going through the same struggle they saw in him, and that they now hear he is still alive. The word "conflict" means a fight or struggle, like that of an athlete in the arena. "Saw" refers to what they witnessed in Philippi; "hear" speaks of the news they receive now.

Paul writes from prison, probably in Rome, although some think of another city. In Acts 16 he was beaten and imprisoned in Philippi, and the believers remembered it. The Philippians were facing opposition for their faith, and Paul encourages them by showing that they are not alone: he is going through the same thing.

For today: if you face pressure or rejection for following Christ, do not think that something is wrong with you. Remember that other believers have gone through the same thing. Seek out someone who has walked that road, ask for advice, and pray together to stay firm.
exp.0:14:
Here is what the verse says: some preach Christ out of envy and rivalry, meaning competition and a desire to compete. But others do it with good will, or in other words, with good intentions.

Paul writes from prison, probably in Rome, to the believers in Philippi. He tells them that his imprisonment helped the gospel advance and encouraged others to speak without fear. Some did it out of rivalry toward him; others did it out of love. Scholars do not agree on exactly who the envious ones were.

For today: check your motives when you serve or share your faith. Ask God for a humble heart, one that does not compete with anyone, and rejoice when Christ is made known, even when it is done by others.
exp.2:5:
Here Paul speaks of two things about his life before he knew Christ. Because of his zeal, his religious enthusiasm, he persecuted the church. And as for keeping the law of Moses outwardly, no one could accuse him of any fault.

Paul writes from prison to the Philippians. He warns them against those who trusted in rituals and human achievements. To show that he is not speaking from ignorance, he presents his religious record, which was impressive. Then he says that he counts all of that as loss compared with knowing Christ.

For today: our religious effort, however sincere, does not save us. We can have much zeal and still be wrong. Let us ask God to teach us to trust in Christ and not in our merits.
exp.0:4:
Paul explains why he thanks God and prays with joy for the Philippians: because of their partnership in the gospel. The word "partnership" means participation or fellowship: they joined Paul in the work of proclaiming Christ. This has been true from the first day until now, that is, from the time they received the message until the moment he is writing.

Paul writes from prison to the church in Philippi, which had supported him with affection and concrete help. Many understand that this partnership included prayers, gifts, and companionship in suffering, although the text here sums it up in a single word.

For today: the gospel is not lived or served alone. Think of a person or group with whom you can work together in the faith, and help them with prayer, time, or steady support, not just now and then.
exp.3:19:
To God, who is our God and Father, belong the glory, the honor, and the praise forever. The phrase "for ever and ever" means "without end," for all eternity. The closing word "Amen" is a confirmation, a way of saying "so be it" or "I truly affirm this."

Paul writes from prison to the church in Philippi. They sent him help through Epaphroditus, and he thanks them. He assures them that God will supply what they lack. After speaking of their generosity and of God's faithfulness, Paul ends this section with praise. For him, every good thing comes from God.

Today we can do the same: when you receive help, an achievement, or a provision, thank the people involved and then offer a simple prayer of praise to God, acknowledging that he is the source of everything.
exp.2:1:
The explanation says believers should be on guard against three kinds of people. "Dogs" is a harsh word; among the Jews it was used for people who were unclean or outside God's people, and here Paul turns it back on those who were teaching wrongly. "Evil workers" are teachers who do work, but damage the faith. "Concision" is a wordplay on "circumcision": it refers to those who insisted on circumcision of the flesh as a requirement for being saved.

Paul writes from prison to the Philippians, whom he loves. There were teachers who said that non-Jews had to be circumcised to please God. Paul answers that God's true family serves in the Spirit and boasts in Christ, not in rituals or their own achievements.

Today, examine what you teach and what you listen to: if anyone adds human requirements to the grace of Christ, be cautious. Trust in Jesus, not in your merits.
exp.3:14:
Paul reminds the Philippians of something they already knew: when he began preaching the gospel and left Macedonia, no other church shared with him in the matter of giving and receiving, meaning supporting him with material help. Only they did so.

Paul writes this letter from prison, and he wants to thank the Philippians for the help they sent him through Epaphroditus. He makes clear that he is not saying this to ask for more, but to show how much he values their constant generosity. The verses that follow explain that they had already helped him even in Thessalonica.

For today: faithfully supporting those who serve God, whether through prayer, offerings, or practical help, is a real way of taking part in his work. And it never goes unnoticed by God.
exp.1:0:
This verse begins a sentence that continues into verse 2. Paul names four things his readers already know: consolation in Christ, the comfort that love brings, fellowship in the Spirit, and tender affection and compassion. The first of these means encouragement or relief; the word for the inner feeling of deep affection refers to the innermost part of the heart; and the word for compassion refers to acts of mercy.

Paul writes to the Philippians from prison. He loves them and thanks them for their support. He reminds them of what they have already received from God, so that in verse 2 he can ask them to live in unity and humility. We do not know the details of any conflicts among them, but the letter repeatedly stresses unity.

For today: before you confront someone, remember how much consolation and mercy you have received from Christ. That remembrance will help you treat with tenderness those who think differently.
exp.1:14:
He says that believers should live in such a way that no one can find anything in them to accuse them of. "Blameless" means without cause for reproach. "Harmless" means whole, pure-hearted, and without duplicity. "A crooked and perverse nation" describes a people morally twisted. "Lights" are bodies that give light, like the stars in the night.

Paul writes to the Philippians from prison. He asks them for unity and humility, and to do everything without complaining or quarreling. He reminds them that God himself is at work in them. His desire is that their lives be a clear witness in a setting that did not know God.

For today: at work, at home, or online, practice a week without complaining or arguing about everything. Respond with calm and honesty. In this way your life shines without your having to say much.
exp.1:9:
This verse says that one day every creature will bow before Jesus, acknowledging his authority. "Bowing the knee" is a gesture of respect and worship. "In heaven, on earth, and under the earth" covers all that has been created; some think it includes angels, living people, and the dead, though it has been interpreted in several ways.

The apostle Paul writes from prison to the Christians in Philippi. He has spoken to them about Jesus, who, being God, made himself humble, obeyed even to death on the cross, and for this reason God exalted him. Paul uses this example to encourage them to live with humility and unity.

For today: if Jesus, being the greatest, chose to serve, you too can do the same. Today look for a concrete way to serve someone without expecting recognition, and remember that Christ is the Lord of your life.
exp.0:20:
For Paul, his whole life revolves around Christ: what he thinks, what he does, and how he lives all have Jesus at the center. That is why dying is not losing but gain, because it would bring him into the presence of Christ. In this older wording, the phrase that means everything will end well or be set free is rendered simply as "well," and the word that means ashamed is rendered simply as "ashamed."

Paul writes to the Philippians from prison. He does not know whether he will be released or executed. Even so, his desire is that Christ be honored in his body, whether through life or through death. In the verses that follow, he explains that living means continuing to bear fruit in his service, and dying would mean being with Christ, which is far better.

Today we can ask what occupies the center of our lives. If it is only work, success, or comfort, then fear of losing them controls us. Today, offer Christ a concrete task and do it to honor him.
exp.0:28:
The explanation says that God has given the Philippians two gifts for Christ's sake: to believe in him and also to suffer for him. The word "given" in the verse above is the key idea here. Paul presents suffering for Christ not as a punishment, but as part of following Jesus.

Paul writes from prison to the church in Philippi. They were facing opposition, and Paul asks them to stay united and not be afraid. He reminds them that he goes through the same struggle, so they are not alone. Scholars do not know in detail what kind of pressure they were under, but it was real.

If today you are criticized, excluded, or find it hard to live faithfully because of your faith, do not see it as a sign that God has abandoned you. Ask him for firmness, and look for the support of other believers so you do not face it alone.
exp.3:5:
This verse says we should not live filled with anxiety about anything. "Anxious" means worried or distressed. Instead, we should make our requests known to God, that is, tell them to him with confidence. We should do this by praying, asking earnestly, and giving thanks.

Paul writes this letter to the believers in Philippi, and he addresses them with affection. Many scholars think he wrote it while in prison, although it is not known for certain where. Even so, he speaks of joy. He reminds them that the Lord is near, and then promises the peace of God.

Today, when a worry takes away your sleep, stop and speak with God. Tell him what you feel, ask for what you need, and give thanks for something specific he has already given you. Then leave the outcome in his hands.
exp.3:1:
Paul asks Evodia and Syntyche, two women in the church, to be of the same mind in the Lord. "I beseech" and "I beseech" are words of gentle but earnest appeal. "Be of the same mind" means sharing the same attitude and purpose, not thinking identically about everything.

Paul writes to the Philippians from prison. He names these two women, which shows that there was a disagreement known to the church. We do not know what the problem was; the letter does not say. Paul recognizes that they worked alongside him in the gospel, and he asks the church to help them be reconciled.

For today: if you have a disagreement with another believer, do not let it grow in silence. Seek out that person, remember what Christ has united you in, and ask a mature brother or sister for help if needed.
exp.3:22:
Paul expresses his wish that the grace of Jesus Christ, that is, his favor and kindness that we do not deserve, be with all the Philippians. "You all" is the plain meaning of the word translated here. "Amen" means "so be it." The final line, "It was written to the Philippians from Rome by Epaphroditus," is a note added in some ancient manuscripts, probably not written by Paul himself.

Paul writes this letter from prison, traditionally placed in Rome, though some scholars think of other cities. He closes with greetings from the believers who are with him, including people from the emperor's household. Epaphroditus had brought the Philippians' help to Paul, and he surely carried this letter back as well.

Today we can end the day by asking for and remembering that we live by the grace of Christ, not by our own strength. And we can bless others with that same hope: sincerely telling someone, "may the grace of God be with you."
exp.2:17:
Paul says that there are many who "walk," that is, who live in a certain way, and that they are "the enemies of the cross of Christ." He had warned them about this many times before, and now he repeats it even with tears.

Paul writes from prison to the Christians in Philippi. He asks them to imitate him and to keep moving forward in faith. Here he warns against those who live differently. The verses that follow speak of people ruled by bodily desires and earthly things. It is not known for certain who they were; some think they were false teachers, others think they were believers who were living badly.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we live in line with the cross: humility, self-giving, and obedience. And when we see someone turning away from Christ, instead of mocking, we can correct them with love, even with tears.
exp.2:7:
He says that Paul counts everything else as loss compared with how great it is to know Jesus, his Lord. For Christ he has lost everything and regards it as dung, that is, worthless rubbish, so that he may gain Christ. "Excellency" means surpassing, of incomparable worth. "Doubtless" means I consider.

Paul writes to the Philippians from prison. Earlier he listed his religious achievements: his zeal, his lineage, and his obedience to the law. He does this to show that he does not trust in these things to be accepted by God. His righteousness does not come from his merits, but from faith in Christ.

Today we can ask ourselves which good things, such as success, prestige, or even our religiousness, we are putting above Jesus. We can ask God that knowing Him be our greatest treasure.
exp.0:7:
Paul says that God is his witness, meaning that God knows his affection is genuine. He says he loves all the Philippians with the deepest feeling of Jesus Christ. The word for those deepest feelings referred to the innermost part of one's emotions, what we would today call the heart. And he says he loves all of them.

Paul writes from prison to the church in Philippi, which had supported him and worked alongside him in the gospel. He wants them to know that he has not forgotten them. His love is not merely human: it reflects the tender love of Christ. That is why he can pray for them with confidence, as he goes on to do in the following verses.

We can ask God to make our love for others sincere and to resemble Christ's love. Today you can choose someone in your church or family, pray for that person, and tell them in simple words that you value them.
exp.1:20:
What it says: Paul states that most of the people around him care first about their own interests and not about what matters to Christ. "Their own" means their own conveniences, and "the things of Christ" refers to his work and to serving others.

Context: Paul is writing from prison and wants to send Timothy to the Philippians. He says no one else shares his concern for them as sincerely. It is not clear whom he means by "all"; probably the coworkers near him at that time, not all Christians. Timothy stands in contrast to them.

For today: Before deciding something, ask yourself: "Does this only benefit me, or does it also help others and honor Christ?" This week, look for a concrete way to serve someone without expecting anything in return.
exp.3:6:
This verse says that the peace that comes from God is so great that we cannot fully grasp it. The meaning of "passeth all understanding" is that it goes beyond what the human mind can explain. This peace will keep our hearts and minds, that is, it will care for and guard them, like a soldier who watches over a city. All of this happens through Christ Jesus, united with him.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians of Philippi while he is in prison. He has just told them not to be anxious, that is, not to live in worry, but to bring their requests to God with thanksgiving. Peace is God's answer to that trusting prayer.

For today: when something worries you, speak to God about it specifically, ask him calmly, and give thanks for what you already have. Then rest, trusting that he will care for your heart, even if the situation has not yet changed.
exp.3:21:
It says that all the believers who were with Paul send greetings to the Philippians. It highlights those "of Cesar's household." The word "saints" does not refer to perfect people, but to those set apart for God, the believers. "Chiefly" means "especially."

Paul writes this letter from prison, and tradition places it in Rome, as the final note indicates. The phrase "of Cesar's household" probably refers to those who served the emperor: slaves, freed people, or officials, not necessarily his family. We do not know their names or how many there were. Paul closes with tenderness, uniting distant churches.

For today: faith can flourish even in difficult or powerful places. If you work or live in an environment hostile or cold toward God, do not lose heart; you can be a light there. And encourage other believers with a sincere greeting, because the unity of the church strengthens it.
exp.3:18:
He says that God will meet the needs of the Philippians. "Will supply" means that he will give or complete what is lacking. "According to his riches" means that God gives in proportion to how much he has, not just a little of what is left over. "In glory by Christ Jesus" points out that this provision comes through Jesus.

Paul writes from prison. The Philippians sent him help through Epaphroditus, and Paul thanks them. He clarifies that he is not asking for more money, but wants their generosity to be a good fruit for them. By saying "my God," he speaks from his own experience: God has cared for him, and will also care for them.

For today: when you give generously, even if you have little, trust that God knows your needs. You can ask him simply and give with peace, without fear of being left with nothing.
exp.3:10:
Paul says he is not speaking out of need. "Want" means poverty, or lacking the basics. He makes clear that he is not asking for anything, because he has learned to be content, that is, to be at peace and satisfied with what he has, whether much or little.

Paul writes this letter from prison to the Philippians, who sent him help through Epaphroditus. He is glad for their care, but he does not want them to think his joy depends on the gift. His peace comes from Christ, and for that reason he can live in any circumstance.

Today we can practice contentment by giving thanks for what we already have before complaining about what is missing. Contentment is learned little by little, and God helps us in that process.
exp.3:8:
This verse says that the Philippians should put into practice what they learned from Paul: his teachings, what they received from him, what they heard him say, and what they saw in his life. The word "do" is the instruction to act on all of it. The promise is that the God of peace will be with them.

Paul writes this letter from prison to the church in Philippi, a church he loves and from which he received help. Earlier he had urged them to think about what is true, just, and pure. Now he calls them to live that out in action, following the example he gave them. Afterward he thanks them for their support and tells them that he has learned to be content in every situation.

Today we can choose a person of faith whose example inspires us and practice this week one specific thing that they live, such as praying steadily or being kind. God's peace grows when we obey, not only when we understand.
exp.0:25:
Paul says he wants to visit the Philippians again so that their rejoicing, their reason for pride and joy in Christ Jesus, may grow. The word "rejoicing" here refers to something a person happily and confidently takes joy in. "By my coming to you again" means: when I return to you.

Paul writes from prison and does not know for certain what will happen to him. Still, he trusts that he will remain alive to help the believers in Philippi grow in their faith. His joy was not in himself: the rejoicing they would have was "in Christ Jesus." He was an instrument, not the center.

For today: when God uses someone to encourage your faith, thank God for that person, but place your joy in Christ. And you too can be a support that helps the joy of others in the Lord grow.
exp.1:4:
This verse invites believers to have the same attitude or way of thinking that Jesus had. The word "mind" means a way of thinking, a disposition of the heart. Paul is not asking only for imitation of actions, but for thinking the way Christ thinks.

Paul writes to the church in Philippi, probably from prison. He has just asked them for unity, humility, and concern for others, avoiding quarrels and the desire to stand out. This verse is the bridge: Jesus is the model of that humility, as the verses that follow show, where it speaks of how he set aside his place of honor to serve.

Today, before you react in an argument or at work, ask yourself: "What attitude would Jesus have here?" Then look for a concrete way to help someone, instead of thinking only about your own interests.
exp.1:12:
This verse says that God is the one who works within you, both giving you the desire to obey him and the strength to do it. The word "works" means "produces" or "acts." "Will" is the desire or willingness, and "do" is the action. God does all this because it pleases him, out of his goodness.

Paul writes from prison to the believers in Philippi, whom he loves dearly. He asks them to live out their faith with seriousness and reverence toward God, even when he is not present. This phrase encourages them: they do not do it alone, because God himself is at work in them.

For today: when you lack the desire or strength to do what is right, do not lose heart. Ask God to give you the desire and the ability, and take one concrete step of obedience today, trusting that he is with you.
exp.2:2:
The explanation says that the true children of God are not those who have only an outward mark, but those who worship God guided by his Spirit, rejoice in Christ Jesus, and do not place their trust in what is human. "Flesh" here means achievements, heritage, or one's own effort. "Mutilation" is a contemptuous way of referring to circumcision done as a requirement for salvation.

Paul writes to the Philippians, probably from prison. He warns them against teachers who demanded that non-Jewish believers be circumcised. Paul tells them that the true sign of God's people is faith and a renewed heart, not a ritual. Right after this, he shows that he himself had more human reasons to boast than anyone.

For today: ask yourself where you place your worth before God, whether in your good works, your church, or your history. Today, rest in Christ and worship God with sincerity.
exp.0:22:
Paul says he is "in a strait betwixt two," that is, pressed between two good options. On one side he desires to depart, a way of speaking about leaving this life, like someone casting off the ropes of a ship or breaking camp. On the other side he wants to be with Christ, and he calls this "far better."

Paul writes from prison to the Christians in Philippi, whom he loves dearly. He does not know whether he will be set free or executed. For him, to live means to serve Christ, and to die means to be with Him. That is why he does not see death as a defeat, but as a gain.

For today: we can face death with peace without ceasing to value life. While we are here, life is an opportunity to love and serve others, trusting that being with Christ is our final hope.
exp.0:1:
This verse is a greeting of blessing. "Gracia sea á vosotros," which means "may grace be with you," refers to God's undeserved favor. The peace in the verse is the deep well-being and calm that come from God. That peace comes from "God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ," that is, from both of them.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Philippi, together with Timothy. It was common for ancient letters to begin with a greeting, but Paul fills it with Christian meaning by joining grace and peace together. He writes warmly to a church he knows well, and he does so from prison, as becomes clear later in the letter.

For today: before beginning the day or a difficult conversation, you can ask for grace and peace for yourself and for others. Remember that we do not produce them ourselves; we receive them from God as a gift.
exp.3:9:
Paul says he rejoiced greatly in the Lord because, at last, the Philippians' care for him had flourished again, that is, had sprung up anew like a plant in spring. The verse's "careful" means they were concerned for him and attentive to his needs. They truly wanted to help him, but they lacked the opportunity.

Paul wrote this letter from prison, and the Philippians had sent him help through Epaphroditus. He does not rebuke them for the time that passed; he recognizes their good intention. Right away he makes clear that his joy does not depend on receiving money, but on his relationship with Christ and on their love.

Today we can learn to look at those who wanted to help us but could not with gratitude and without reproach. We can also ask ourselves whom we can reach out to now, before more time passes.
exp.1:24:
Paul says it seemed necessary to send Epaphroditus back. He describes him with five titles: a brother in the faith, a fellow worker in the work, a companion in the fight (someone who struggles alongside you, like a soldier), the messenger of the Philippians, and the one who ministered, that is, the one who looked after Paul's needs.

Paul writes from prison, and the Philippians had sent Epaphroditus with a gift to help him. Epaphroditus became seriously ill, and when the Philippians heard of it, Paul sends him home to reassure them and to honor his service. We do not know exactly what his illness was.

For today: value and thank those who serve quietly, and encourage them with specific words. Perhaps today you could write to someone or tell them: "Thank you for your service. God sees it, and so do I."
exp.2:14:
Paul says that those of us who are "as many as be perfect," that is, mature in the faith, should think the same way he does: pressing on toward the goal in Christ. The verb "think" in this verse means to think or to hold the same attitude. And if someone thinks differently about something, God himself will make that clear to them.

Paul writes to the Philippians from prison. Just before this, he confessed that he has not yet reached the goal and that he keeps pressing forward. That is why he calls the mature "perfect," since they recognize that they still have room to grow. Some scholars see a touch of irony here; others see a sincere use of the word.

For today: stay humble and keep growing, without thinking you have already arrived. And when someone thinks differently from you about secondary matters, pray and trust that God can show the truth to everyone, including you.
exp.2:11:
Paul says he has not yet reached the goal. The word "attained" means gained or received, and "perfect" means mature, complete. The phrase "I follow after" means pressing on with effort. He keeps moving forward to take hold of that for which Jesus Christ took hold of him: that is, Christ reached him first, and now Paul responds to that call.

Paul writes this letter from prison to the church at Philippi, whom he loves dearly. He has just said that he wants to know Christ, the power of his resurrection, and his sufferings. Although he is an apostle with much experience, he shows humility: he sees himself on the way, not at the finish. Scholars debate a little what exactly he means by "perfect," but the general sense is final maturity.

Today we can stop comparing ourselves to others or feeling defeated by our failures. If you are growing in faith, keep walking with steadiness, trusting that Christ has already taken you by the hand.
exp.0:27:
Paul tells the Philippians not to be frightened by those who oppose them. He is saying that their fearlessness is a sign to their opponents, and that this fearlessness is evidence that they have salvation and that this salvation comes from God, while the opposition of others points to their fate apart from Christ.

Paul writes from prison to a church that was under pressure because of its faith. He asks them to live in a way that is worthy of the gospel, united and steadfast. Scholars do not agree on exactly who the opponents were, but the text shows that there was real resistance and that Paul wanted to encourage them.

Today, when someone mocks your faith or pressures you, you do not have to respond with fear or anger. Stand firm, be kind, and lean on your brothers and sisters, trusting that God sustains his own.
exp.2:18:
This verse describes people who live as enemies of the cross of Christ. Their end is destruction, that is, final ruin. Their god is their belly: they let their desires and appetites rule them. Their glory is in their shame: they take pride in things that are disgraceful. They mind earthly things: they think only about the things of this world.

Paul writes from prison to the Christians in Philippi. He asks them to imitate his example and warns, with tears, about those who live badly. It is not known exactly who they were; some think they were false teachers, others believers who lived without discipline. Then Paul reminds them that our citizenship is in heaven.

For today: ask yourself what controls your life, whether pleasure, money, or comfort. Ask God to set your heart on Christ and on what is eternal.
exp.0:0:
Paul and Timothy introduce themselves as servants of Jesus Christ, that is, people who belong to Christ and obey him. They write to all the saints in Philippi, a word meaning set apart for God, not people who are perfect. These believers are in Christ Jesus. They also greet the bishops (overseers or pastors) and the deacons (those who serve).

Paul writes this letter from prison, as the book itself suggests. Philippi was a city in Macedonia where he had founded a church. Although Timothy appears in the greeting, the rest of the letter uses "I," so it is understood that Paul is the main author. He writes with affection to a church that was very dear to him.

For today: Your worth does not depend on your achievements, but on being in Christ. Remember that you are part of his people, and serve others with humility, whatever your place in the church.
exp.1:15:
Paul says that the Philippians should hold forth the word of life, that is, hold firmly to the gospel message that gives life. Thus, on the day of Christ, when Jesus returns and judges, Paul will be able to rejoice, because his effort will not have been in vain. Running and laboring speak of his dedication and weariness for the gospel.

Paul writes from prison to the church in Philippi, which he loves very much. He asks them to live without complaints or quarrels, shining like lights in the midst of a corrupt society. His desire is to see that his ministry bears lasting fruit in them. Some understand that holding forth can also mean offering; both ideas fit.

Today we can remain firm in the Word of God, reading it consistently and living it at home and at work. In this way our lives will be a testimony that points to Christ.
exp.0:10:
He says Paul wants the Philippians to be filled with "fruits of righteousness," that is, with a life that shows the goodness and uprightness God produces in a person. Those fruits do not come from oneself but "through Jesus Christ." And the goal of it all is the glory of God and the praise of God; the word "praise" here is an older way of saying praise, meaning exaltation given to God.

Paul writes this letter from prison, and in these verses he prays for his friends in Philippi. He asks that their love grow with knowledge and good judgment, so that they live with sincerity until the day of Christ. Right after this, Paul will tell them that his imprisonment has helped the gospel move forward.

For today: do not seek only to behave well by your own strength. Ask Jesus to form in you attitudes such as patience, honesty, and love, and aim for the good you do to point toward honoring God, not toward making yourself look good.
exp.0:18:
Paul says he is confident that what is happening to him, that is, the imprisonment and its hardships, will turn out to his good. The word used for this outcome can be understood as deliverance or as the final good, and scholars read it in both ways. He believes this will happen because of two things: the prayers of the Philippians and the constant help of the Spirit of Jesus Christ.

Paul writes from prison, and some were preaching Christ with good motives while others did so with doubtful ones. Even so, he rejoices that Christ is being proclaimed. His confidence does not rest on his circumstances but on God working through the prayers of his people and through the Spirit.

Today, when you go through a trial, pray and ask others to pray for you. Trust that the Spirit sustains you and that God can bring something good out of it, even if you cannot yet see how.
exp.1:21:
The explanation says that the Philippians already know Timothy's proof, that is, his character tested over time. Paul affirms that Timothy has served him the way a son serves his father, working together to proclaim the gospel. Words to note: the Philippians "know" him (the verse reads "ye know") and the wording refers to what Timothy has proved in service.

Paul writes this letter from prison, according to tradition and what the text indicates, and he wants to send Timothy to Philippi. Earlier he said that almost everyone looks out for their own interests, so he highlights Timothy as someone trustworthy who genuinely cares for them. In this way he commends his co-worker to the church.

For today: good character is shown by serving faithfully, not only by words. Look for a concrete way to help in your church or family, even if no one recognizes it, and do it with humility and faithfulness.
exp.3:16:
Paul makes clear that he is not asking for or seeking gifts. "Gifts" here means donations or contributions. What he desires is "fruit that may abound to your account," meaning that the good the Philippians do would build up in their favor, like a spiritual profit that God records for them.

Paul writes from prison to the church in Philippi, which had supported him with money from the very beginning. He has just thanked them for the help brought by Epaphroditus. So that he would not seem to be after something for himself, he explains that his joy does not lie in the money, but in what that generosity means for them before God.

For today: when you give or help, do it without pressure or show, trusting that God sees and values your generosity. And if you receive help, thank the giver by looking at the heart behind it.
exp.2:12:
Paul says that he does not regard himself as someone who has already reached the goal. The phrase "I count not myself" means "I do not think of myself" or "I do not consider myself" as having arrived. His focus is on one thing: not dwelling on "those things which are behind" and "reaching forth unto those things which are before," like a runner who stretches out his whole body to move forward.

Paul writes this letter to the Philippians from prison. Earlier he spoke of what he had achieved as a respected Jew, and said that he considered all of it loss compared with knowing Christ. Now he makes clear that he is still on the way and has not yet reached full maturity.

Today we can let go of both the failures and the successes of the past, which sometimes hold us back. Ask God to help you take one concrete step toward Christ today.
exp.2:13:
Paul says that he keeps pressing forward toward the goal, like a runner who keeps his eyes on the finish line. The "mark" is the point he is heading toward, and the "prize" is what he will receive when he reaches it. The "high calling" means the call from above, which comes from God through Christ Jesus.

Paul writes from prison to the Philippians. He makes clear that he does not consider himself perfect and does not believe he has already arrived. After speaking of what he has left behind, his former religious life, he presents himself as someone who is still on the way. Scholars debate exactly what the prize consists of; many think it is the fullness of living with Christ.

Today we can stop carrying old failures or achievements and ask ourselves: what small step can I take today to keep following Christ?
exp.0:26:
The explanation says that believers should live in a way that is worthy of the gospel. Paul wants to know, whether he comes to see them or is far away, that they stand firm, united in one spirit and striving together, like a team, for the faith of the gospel.

Paul writes to the Philippians from prison. He has just told them that he hopes to see them again. What matters most to him is that, with him or without him, the church remain faithful and united, even when it faces opposition, as the verses that follow show.

For today: take care of the unity of your church or your family. Before arguing over small things, ask yourself whether the way you speak and treat others reflects the gospel. Live the same way when people see you as when they do not.
exp.1:23:
Paul says he trusts in the Lord, that is, he hopes that from God he will soon be able to visit the Philippians.

Paul writes from prison, and so he cannot go whenever he likes. He has already said that he will send Timothy, the young man who served him like a son to a father, as soon as he sees how his situation turns out. Here he adds his personal hope of going himself. Notice that he does not place his trust in his own plans or in the judges, but in the Lord. We do not know with certainty whether he was able to make that journey afterward.

For today: make your plans with hope, but place them in God's hands. You can say: "This is what I want to do, Lord, and I trust in you, whatever the outcome."
exp.0:2:
Paul says that he thanks God every time he remembers the Philippians. "I thank my God upon every remembrance of you" means giving thanks, and the word "upon" in that phrase refers to the time when he remembers them, so it can be read as "every time I remember you." When Paul thinks of them, his heart is filled with gratitude toward God.

Paul writes this letter from prison, and Timothy is included in the greeting. The Philippians had supported him in his work for the gospel. That is why he begins with thanks and affection, before turning to other matters. He says "my God," which shows a personal relationship with Him.

Today we can do the same: think of the people God has placed in our lives, such as family, friends, or brothers and sisters in the church, and give thanks to God for them. This week, remember someone who has helped you in your faith, thank God for that person, and if you can, write them a few words of encouragement.
exp.2:6:
He says that everything Paul once considered an advantage, such as his background, his religion, and his good record, he now sees as loss. The sentence with the old wording is simply rendered as: "I have counted them" is old-fashioned language meaning "I have considered them." Those things that were gain are things of value, and "loss" refers to things that are not worth keeping. The reason he gives is for the sake of Christ.

Paul writes from prison to the believers in Philippi. He has just mentioned his Jewish credentials, which impressed many people. He mentions them because some teachers trusted those merits to please God. Paul shows that, although he had all of that, valuing Christ was far more important.

For today: ask yourself what you rest your worth before God on, whether achievements, reputation, or good behavior. Those things can be good, but they do not save you. Put Christ first and let Him be your greatest treasure.
exp.1:28:
Paul asks the Philippians to receive Epaphroditus in the Lord, that is, as a brother in the faith, and with great joy. He also asks them to honor and value people like him. The word "receive" in the verse is the same as "receive" in your reading, and "hold in reputation" means to hold such people in high regard.

Paul writes from prison. The Philippians had sent Epaphroditus to help him, and there he fell seriously ill. Now Paul is sending him back home, and he wants him to be welcomed well, since he risked his life serving the work of Christ.

Today we can notice the people who serve faithfully, sometimes without being seen, in the church or the family. A word of gratitude, a visit, or a genuine sign of affection can encourage them greatly and reflect the love of Christ.
exp.1:5:
This verse says that Christ, from eternity, existed in the nature of God, and that being equal with God was not something he had taken by force. Taking something that belongs to another is what "robbery" means here. Christ did not seize something that was not his: that equality was his own. Some understand that he did not regard it as something to be grasped, and modern translations express it this way.
