The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Philippi from prison. He asks them for unity and humility, and not to seek only their own advantage. He sets Jesus before them as an example: if he, being God, did not cling to his position, they too should not cling to theirs.

Today we might ask ourselves: in what situation do I cling to my place, my reasoning, or my comfort? This week, choose to serve someone without asking for recognition, following the mind of Christ.
exp.1:7:
This verse says that Jesus, already made a human being, humbled himself. He obeyed God all the way to the last step: death, and not just any kind of death, but death on a cross, a painful and shameful way to die. The phrase about being found in the appearance of a man means that he was seen and lived as a true human being.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Philippi, from prison. He asks them for unity and humility among themselves. To make this point, he presents Christ to them as an example: though equal to God, he came down to serve and to sacrifice. Afterward, God exalted him.

Today we can follow that example in everyday life: giving way in an argument, serving without seeking applause, forgiving first. Humility is not weakness; it is loving as Jesus loved, trusting that God cares for those who surrender themselves to Him.
exp.0:16:
This verse speaks of a group of people who preached Christ with a good heart. They did it out of love, that is, out of affection for Paul and for the gospel. They knew that God had appointed him to be in prison in order to stand up for the gospel, that is, to present it and uphold it before those who opposed it.

Paul writes from prison, probably in Rome, though some scholars have suggested another place. He tells the Philippians that while he is in chains, some preach out of envy and rivalry, wanting to make his situation harder, and others do it with sincere love. He wants them to understand that his imprisonment does not stop the gospel.

For today: examine why you serve God. Ask him that your motives be love for Christ and for people, and not competition or self-display. And rejoice when others do the work well.
exp.1:19:
Paul says he has no one like Timothy. "Likeminded" means that he thinks and feels the same as Paul, with the same heart. "Genuine affection" is a real fondness, and "naturally care" means attentive and concerned for the good of the Philippians.

Paul writes from prison, probably in Rome, though some think of another place. He wants to send Timothy to Philippi to learn how they are doing and to be encouraged by good news. He recommends him because Timothy truly cares for them, while others look out for their own interests.

For today: ask yourself whether your service springs from sincere love for people or from your own convenience. Today you can truly care for someone: call them, listen to them, pray for them, and help them with something concrete, without expecting anything in return.
exp.3:17:
Paul says that he already has everything he needs, and more. He is content with what the Philippians sent through Epaphroditus. Using the language of the older Bible, he calls that gift a fragrant aroma (a pleasing smell) and an offering Dios receives gladly, a sacrifice acceptable to God. The old word that is rendered "but" in some versions simply means "but", and the old form "you sent" means "they sent".

Paul writes from prison and thanks the church of Philippi for its financial help. He makes clear that he is not asking for more, but that he wants them to receive the fruit of their generosity. Epaphroditus was the messenger who brought the offering. Paul uses the language of Old Testament worship to show that giving out of love is also worship.

Today we can see that helping others, whether a missionary, a pastor, or a needy neighbor, is not just fulfilling a duty. God receives it as an act of worship. Give with simplicity and joy.
exp.2:20:
He says that Jesus Christ, when he returns, will change our weak and limited body so that it becomes like his glorious body. "Body of our humiliation" means our fragile body, the one that suffers and dies. "Operation" means power at work. "To subject all things to himself" means to place everything under his authority. The same power that rules the universe will transform our body.

Paul writes to the believers in Philippi, probably from prison. Earlier he spoke of people who live only for bodily pleasures and the things of this world. By contrast, he reminds us that Christians belong to heaven and are waiting for their Savior. Their hope is not in earthly things but in what Christ will do.

For today: when sickness, exhaustion, or age discourages you, remember that your present body is not the last word. Care for your body with gratitude, but place your hope in Christ and live looking toward what is eternal.
exp.1:26:
He says that Epaphroditus was very ill, so ill that he came close to dying. But God had mercy on him, that is, He healed him and did not let him die. Paul adds that this mercy was also for him, so that he would not have sorrow upon sorrow, that is, pain piled on top of pain.

Paul writes from prison to the Philippians. Epaphroditus had brought their gift to Paul and stayed on to serve him. He fell ill, and the Philippians heard about it and were troubled. Paul sends him back so that they may see him well and rejoice.

For today: recognize the hand of God in healings and relief, great or small, and give thanks for them. And do not hide your pain: Paul admits his sorrow honestly. Walk alongside those who suffer, as Epaphroditus did.
exp.2:0:
He says that what remains for them to do, brothers, is to rejoice in the Lord. The word "finally" means "as for the rest" or "in conclusion." "Rejoice" means "be glad." Paul adds that repeating the same things to them does not bother him, because for them it is "safe," that is, it gives them firmness and protection.

The apostle Paul speaks, writing to the Christians in Philippi, probably from prison. Some scholars think "the same things" refers to the joy he has just mentioned, and others to the warnings that come next against those who taught trusting in the flesh. It may include both ideas.

Today: repeating what is essential is not boring, it is wise. Make it a habit to return each day to the basic truths of the gospel and to thank God. That joy in the Lord gives you stability when circumstances change.
exp.1:25:
This verse says that Epaphroditus longed to see all the Philippians. It also says he was deeply distressed, because they had heard that he had been sick. To be "full of heaviness" means he was greatly troubled and burdened.

Paul writes from prison to the church in Philippi. Epaphroditus had brought the Philippians' gift to Paul and had become so ill that he nearly died. Paul explains why he is sending him back: Epaphroditus did not want anyone to worry, and now he wants to put their minds at ease and be reunited with them.

Epaphroditus was more distressed by the worry of others than by his own illness. We can follow his example today: when someone cares for us or prays for us, let us think also of their hearts and let them know how we are doing. In this way we love one another with tenderness and sincerity.
exp.2:10:
Paul says he hopes to attain the resurrection of the dead, and he expresses it with the words "if by any means," which in today's English would be "somehow, if possible." The word "attain" here is an older, more formal way of saying "reach." This does not sound like doubt about salvation, but rather humility and seriousness. Some believe he is speaking of the resurrection of believers in general, and others of a special fullness. The Bible does not fully clarify this.

Paul writes to the Philippians from prison. He has just said that everything he once valued he now considers loss because of knowing Christ. He wants to share in Christ's sufferings and death, with the hope of rising with Him. His confidence is not in his own merits, but in the righteousness that comes from God through faith.

Today we can live with our eyes fixed on the hope of the resurrection. That helps us endure trials with patience, without boasting of our achievements, and trusting in Christ each day.

sum.0: Paul, who is in prison, sends greetings to the church in Philippi. He thanks God for their partnership in the gospel and prays that their love will grow in knowledge and wisdom. He is glad that his chains have helped the gospel spread, and he says that for him, to live is Christ and to die is gain. He encourages them to live in a way that is worthy of the gospel, to stand united, and not to be afraid, even when they suffer.
sum.3: Paul encourages the Philippians to stand firm, to live in unity, to rejoice in the Lord, and not to be anxious, but to pray with thanksgiving, since God's peace will guard their hearts. He teaches them to think about what is good and pure, and he thanks them for their help, trusting that God will supply everything they lack.
sum.2: Paul warns against those who put their trust in human achievements. He explains that he gave up his entire religious record to know Christ and to receive the righteousness that comes through faith. He admits he has not yet reached the goal, but he keeps pressing on toward the prize. He invites readers to live as citizens of heaven, eagerly waiting for Jesus to transform our bodies.
sum.1: Paul asks the Philippians to live in unity, with humility and love, looking out for one another as Christ did. Christ humbled himself, even to the point of death on a cross, and God therefore exalted him. Paul encourages them to work out their salvation without complaining, shining like lights in the world. He also tells them that he is sending Timothy and Epaphroditus, and asks that they be received with joy.
